Sunday, 13 July. The family has gone to the grandmother’s village, 40 kilometres from Iași. Radu, back from the seaside, has come too. After lunch, Ioana, Julien and Radu are sitting in the shade in the yard.
Julien, I owe you an apology. For the sentences I had taught you…
Eight extra sarmale, Radu! I nearly died eating!
I know, I know. But you learnt Romanian while having fun, didn’t you? It’s the best method.
Radu, you’re impossible! Look, Granny’s calling us, waving her apron.
She wants us to go and pick cherries. She says if we pick them now, we can make jam this evening.
I’m coming! I love this place. Arriving this morning, I felt as if I was stepping into a painting.
It’s the house where my mother grew up. She used to come and fetch water from the well, singing, every morning.
And that hill over there, with the big tree?
That’s the old walnut tree. Dad told me he often used to go up there when he was young. I don’t know why.
(coughing, looking at Julien) Ahem… I know why.
(quickly) Ioana, what if we went up there this evening, at sunset? We’d see the whole village.
Why not? But you’ve been acting strangely for a week. You keep smiling when you look at me.
It’s your father’s țuică. It has side effects.
(laughing) Come on, cherries! If we didn’t hurry, Granny would come and fetch us herself.

Take the “nous” form of the present, remove “-ons” and add “-ant”. Put “en” in front. It’s the equivalent of the English “-ing” form (walking, speaking), often with “while” or “by”.
Only three exceptions: être → en étant, avoir → en ayant, savoir → en sachant.
The gerund has three main meanings. Careful: the subject of the gerund is the SAME as that of the main verb.
En partant tôt, on arrivera à l’heure.
If you leave early, you’ll arrive on time.
En arrivant, j’ai vu la maison.
When I arrived, I saw the house.
“Tout en” + gerund emphasises simultaneity or a contrast: “Il souriait tout en pleurant.” (He was smiling, even though he was crying.)
“J’ai vu Ioana en sortant” = I was the one going out when I saw her. If Ioana was going out, you say: “J’ai vu Ioana qui sortait.”

Going up the hill at sunset
Dad told me he had often gone up there.
At about eight in the evening, the sun was starting to go down behind the fields. Julien had checked his pocket ten times. The little blue box was still there.
They set off walking slowly, hand in hand. They crossed the garden, where the hens were already settling down for the night, then the little bridge over the stream.
On the way up, Ioana talked about her childhood. In summer she used to come here with Radu. They picked cherries while squabbling, and their grandmother called them, shouting from the kitchen.

Julien listened to her without really hearing. His heart was pounding so hard that he was afraid she would hear it. He was thinking of Henri, who had prepared a long speech and forgotten it. He was thinking of Dan, who had climbed this same hill thirty years earlier.

When they reached the top, they sat down under the old walnut tree. From there you could see the whole village: the red roofs, the church bell tower, the smoke rising from the chimneys. And in the distance, the road leading to Iași.
“It’s magnificent,” said Ioana. “I understand why my father used to come up here. But I still don’t know why he would never explain it to me.”

Julien took a deep breath. He had rehearsed his sentence for a week. He had written it in his notebook, between two scores. But at that moment, looking at Ioana in the orange evening light, he forgot everything. Exactly like Henri.
So he took the box out of his pocket, opened it, and said simply, in a trembling voice: “Will you?”
Ioana looked at the ring. She recognised the little green stone: Hélène had shown it to her in a photo one day, while telling her story. She put her hands over her mouth. She couldn’t speak any more.
“Hélène gave it to me,” Julien explained. “She said that if one day I wanted to ask you, she’d like you to wear it. As if Henri’s promise had finally been kept.”
“Yes,” said Ioana, crying. “Yes, yes, yes!” And then she laughed, still crying, because she no longer knew if she was sad or happy. Happy, of course. Happier than she had ever been.
Julien put the ring on her finger. It fitted perfectly, as if it had been made for her.

They stayed under the walnut tree for a long time, without saying anything, watching the sun disappear. Then, on the way back down, they heard applause. The whole family was in the garden: Dan, Elena, Radu, the grandmother, and even the cousin with the țuică.
“You all knew?!” cried Ioana. “Everyone knew,” replied Elena with a smile. “Except you.” The grandmother came over and kissed Julien on both cheeks. Then she said something in Romanian.
“What is she saying?” asked Julien. Ioana translated, laughing through her tears: “She says that now you’re part of the family. And that tomorrow she’ll make you sarmale. Lots of sarmale.”

Later, during the night, Julien’s phone buzzed. It was a message from Madame Bernard, who had heard the news from Elena: “Hélène knows. She cried, she laughed, and she asked for Henri’s waltz to be played at your wedding. She says she’ll dance, even with her stick. Victor sends his love too.”
Julien showed the message to Ioana. They fell asleep smiling, Ioana’s hand on the pillow, with the little green stone shining in the dark.

Ioana sends a message to her friends’ group in Lyon the next morning. Listen to the text twice, then read it aloud. At the end, answer 4 questions.
Good morning, everyone! I have some news to tell you, and I’m still trembling a little as I write.
Last night, in my grandmother’s village, Julien asked me to go up the hill where there’s an old walnut tree.
When we got to the top, he was as white as a sheet. I thought he was ill! He was out of breath and his hands were trembling.
Then he took out a little blue box. He didn’t kneel. He just said, smiling: “Will you?”
I said yes, crying. And laughing. Both at the same time!
